title: Anatomy of a Cell
description: The basic unit of life and its working parts

concepts.title: The Cell Membrane
concepts.contentHtml:
Every cell is enclosed by a cell membrane — a double layer of fat molecules called a phospholipid bilayer.

It's selectively permeable: small molecules like oxygen and water cross freely, but large or charged molecules need special transport proteins. This control is essential — without it, cell contents would simply diffuse into the surroundings.

Embedded in the membrane are proteins acting as channels, pumps, receptors, and ID badges. The membrane is less a wall and more a sophisticated checkpoint.

concepts.title: The Nucleus and DNA
concepts.contentHtml:
The nucleus is the cell's control center. It contains DNA — the molecular blueprint that codes for every protein the cell makes.

DNA is bundled into chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in every body cell.

Only eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have nuclei. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm — they're simpler and far more ancient.

concepts.title: Mitochondria and Other Organelles
concepts.contentHtml:
Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. They convert food (glucose) into ATP, the energy currency that powers every cellular process.

Curiously, mitochondria have their own DNA and were likely once free-living bacteria swallowed by an ancestral cell — the endosymbiotic theory.

Other key organelles: ribosomes (build proteins), endoplasmic reticulum (protein/lipid factory), Golgi apparatus (packaging and shipping), lysosomes (waste disposal).

title: Cell Division
description: How one cell becomes two — and why it matters

concepts.title: The Cell Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells don't divide constantly — they cycle through phases.

Interphase is the long working phase where the cell grows and copies its DNA. It's split into G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), and G2 (preparation).

M phase is the brief division phase, including mitosis (nucleus splits) and cytokinesis (cell splits in two).

Checkpoints control the cycle. When checkpoints fail, cells may divide uncontrollably — this is the cellular basis of cancer.

concepts.title: Mitosis — Cloning
concepts.contentHtml:
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells. It's how you grow, heal wounds, and replace dead cells.

The phases are P-M-A-T: Prophase (DNA condenses), Metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), Anaphase (sister chromatids pull apart), Telophase (nuclei reform).

Each daughter receives a complete copy of the parent's 46 chromosomes. No genetic variation is introduced — this is precision copying.

concepts.title: Meiosis — Sex Cells
concepts.contentHtml:
Meiosis produces sex cells (sperm and eggs). Unlike mitosis, it has two divisions and produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosomes (23 in humans, not 46).

This is essential: when sperm and egg fuse at fertilization, the resulting cell gets back to 46.

Meiosis also shuffles genes through 'crossing over' — a key source of genetic variation. This is why siblings (except identical twins) are genetically different despite the same parents.

title: Cell Transport
description: How molecules cross the cell membrane

concepts.title: Diffusion and Osmosis
concepts.contentHtml:
Molecules naturally spread from areas of high concentration to low concentration — this is diffusion. Drop dye in water: it spreads on its own, no energy required.

Osmosis is the special case of water diffusing across a membrane.

Cells exploit diffusion: oxygen flows in (high outside, low inside) and CO₂ flows out (high inside, low outside) automatically.

Both processes are passive — they happen without the cell spending ATP. They run downhill on the concentration gradient.

concepts.title: Active Transport
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometimes cells need to move molecules against their concentration gradient — uphill. This requires energy.

Active transport uses ATP to power membrane proteins called pumps that grab molecules on one side and release them on the other.

The most famous example is the sodium-potassium pump, which keeps cells low in sodium and high in potassium. Your nerves and muscles depend on this gradient — a third of your resting energy goes to maintaining it.

concepts.title: Endocytosis and Exocytosis
concepts.contentHtml:
For very large cargo, the cell membrane itself wraps around material to bring it in or push it out.

Endocytosis: the membrane folds inward, pinches off, and engulfs an external particle. White blood cells eat bacteria this way (phagocytosis).

Exocytosis: vesicles inside the cell merge with the membrane and dump their contents outside. This is how neurons release neurotransmitters and how cells secrete proteins.

Both are active processes requiring energy and elaborate machinery.

title: Cellular Energy
description: How cells extract and store usable energy

concepts.title: ATP — The Energy Currency
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells don't burn glucose directly to power their machinery — they convert energy into ATP (adenosine triphosphate), then spend ATP whenever energy is needed.

ATP works like a rechargeable battery. Breaking off one phosphate releases energy and produces ADP. Adding it back (using glucose energy) recharges to ATP.

Your body recycles your body-weight equivalent of ATP every day. The pool stays small but cycles fast.

concepts.title: Cellular Respiration
concepts.contentHtml:
Cellular respiration is how cells extract energy from glucose, using oxygen, and produce ATP.

Overall: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + ATP

It happens in stages: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm), the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain (in mitochondria). The chain produces the most ATP — about 30 per glucose.

Without oxygen, cells fall back on fermentation, which yields far less ATP. This is why aerobic exercise is sustainable and sprinting (anaerobic) burns out fast.

concepts.title: Photosynthesis — Reverse Engineering
concepts.contentHtml:
Plants do the opposite of respiration. Photosynthesis uses light energy to build glucose from CO₂ and water:

6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂

This happens in chloroplasts, organelles with their own DNA — likely descended from ancient cyanobacteria (another endosymbiosis story).

Photosynthesis is why we have an oxygen atmosphere at all. Before the Great Oxygenation Event ~2.4 billion years ago, Earth's air was almost oxygen-free. Cyanobacteria changed that — and changed everything.

title: Cell Communication
description: How cells talk to each other — and what happens when they don't

concepts.title: Receptors and Ligands
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells communicate via chemical signals. A ligand is the signal molecule (hormone, neurotransmitter, growth factor). A receptor is the protein on the target cell that binds it.

The fit is highly specific — receptors are like locks; ligands are keys. Insulin only binds insulin receptors; adrenaline only binds adrenergic receptors.

When binding occurs, the receptor changes shape and triggers events inside the cell — even though the signal itself never enters.

concepts.title: Signal Transduction
concepts.contentHtml:
The journey from receptor activation to cellular response is called signal transduction.

Typically a cascade: receptor activates an enzyme, which activates more enzymes, which activate more — amplifying the original signal massively.

One adrenaline molecule can ultimately mobilize millions of glucose molecules from liver cells. This amplification is why hormones can act in tiny concentrations.

The cascade also lets the cell integrate multiple signals before deciding to act.

concepts.title: Cancer — Broken Signaling
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells normally divide only when growth signals tell them to. Cancer is what happens when this checkpoint system breaks.

Mutations in oncogenes (growth-promoting) or tumor suppressor genes (growth-restricting) can lock the 'divide' signal ON or break the 'don't divide' signal.

The cell now divides without instructions, ignoring the body's signals to stop. It also resists the orderly self-destruction (apoptosis) that normally clears damaged cells.

Cancer treatments increasingly target specific broken pathways rather than killing all dividing cells indiscriminately.

title: The Cytoskeleton
description: The cell's mechanical scaffold and motor system

concepts.title: Three Filament Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
The cytoskeleton has three main components:

• Actin filaments (~7 nm) provide cell shape, drive crawling motility, contract muscles. Treadmill — assemble at one end, disassemble at the other.
• Microtubules (~25 nm) are highways for cargo transport, build the mitotic spindle, and form cilia/flagella.
• Intermediate filaments (~10 nm) provide mechanical strength — keratin in skin and hair, vimentin in many tissues, lamins lining the nucleus.

concepts.title: Motors on the Tracks
concepts.contentHtml:
Specialized motor proteins walk along cytoskeletal filaments. Myosins on actin (mostly toward + end). Kinesins and dyneins on microtubules (typically + and − end directed, respectively).

Motors haul vesicles, organelles, mRNA. Each takes ~8 nm steps powered by ATP hydrolysis. Hundreds of cargo-specific motor variants exist in mammals.

Defects in motors or tracks cause disease — neuropathy, ciliopathies (polycystic kidney disease, primary ciliary dyskinesia), some forms of cancer.

concepts.title: Cell Migration
concepts.contentHtml:
Crawling cells extend an actin-based protrusion (lamellipodium) at the leading edge, form new adhesions with the substrate, contract the cell body forward via myosin, and release rear adhesions.

Critical in development (cells migrate to organize tissues), wound healing (fibroblasts and immune cells move to repair), and cancer metastasis (tumor cells exploit the same machinery to invade).

Many cancer drugs and developmental signals target migration. Anti-metastatic strategies are an active research goal.

concepts.title: The Phases
concepts.contentHtml:
The eukaryotic cell cycle has four phases: G1 (growth, response to signals), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (preparation for mitosis), M (mitosis, then cytokinesis).

Cells can exit the cycle into G0 — quiescent state. Most cells in your body are in G0. Stem cells, immune cells responding to infection, and tumor cells move out of G0 into the cycle.

concepts.title: Cyclins and Checkpoints
concepts.contentHtml:
Cyclins rise and fall during the cell cycle. They activate CDKs (cyclin-dependent kinases) that drive progression — different cyclin/CDK pairs at each transition.

Checkpoints halt the cycle if something is wrong: G1/S checkpoint (DNA damage, growth signals), G2/M checkpoint (DNA replication complete?), spindle checkpoint (chromosomes properly attached?).

Hartwell, Nurse, and Hunt shared the 2001 Medicine Nobel for the cyclin/CDK story. The system is conserved from yeast to humans.

concepts.title: p53 and Cancer
concepts.contentHtml:
p53 is the most-studied tumor suppressor — sometimes called 'guardian of the genome'. Activated by DNA damage, it triggers cell-cycle arrest (giving repair time) or apoptosis (if damage is too severe).

p53 is mutated in about half of all cancers. Without functioning p53, damaged cells continue dividing — accumulating more mutations.

p53-restoring therapies (small molecules that reactivate mutant p53, MDM2 inhibitors that stabilize wild-type p53) are in clinical trials. The cell-cycle/cancer connection is the core of modern oncology.

concepts.title: Apoptosis
concepts.contentHtml:
Apoptosis is programmed cell death — clean, regulated, neighborhood-friendly. Cells condense, fragment into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, and are engulfed by phagocytes without inflammation.

Triggered by external death signals (Fas/FasL — extrinsic pathway) or internal stress (DNA damage activating p53 → mitochondrial cytochrome c release — intrinsic pathway). Both pathways converge on caspase enzymes.

Essential during development (sculpts fingers from web-fingered embryo), tissue homeostasis, and immune regulation. Failure of apoptosis contributes to cancer; excessive apoptosis to neurodegenerative disease.

concepts.title: Necrosis & Pyroptosis
concepts.contentHtml:
Necrosis is unregulated cell death from severe injury — cells swell, burst, release contents, trigger inflammation. Damaging to surrounding tissue.

Pyroptosis is regulated inflammatory death — triggered by infection. Inflammasomes activate gasdermin proteins that pore the membrane, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines. Recruits immune defenders.

Necroptosis, ferroptosis, autophagy-dependent death — the 'death pathway' catalog has expanded greatly. Each is regulated; each can be targeted therapeutically.

concepts.title: Senescence
concepts.contentHtml:
Some cells stop dividing without dying — they become senescent. Triggered by telomere shortening, DNA damage, oncogene activation. Senescent cells are metabolically active and secrete inflammatory factors (the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, SASP).

Senescent cells accumulate with age and may drive aspects of aging itself. Senolytics — drugs that selectively kill senescent cells — extend healthspan in mouse models. Early human trials are underway.
